cards.front: Enhancers are stretches of {{c1::noncoding DNA}} that switch a gene on in particular tissues.
cards.quote: Pitx1's expression is set by several enhancers (stretches of noncoding DNA that switch a gene on in particular tissues).

cards.front: In Paxton Lake benthic sticklebacks, which genetic change goes with loss of the pelvis, and what about Pitx1 stays intact?
cards.back: A deletion in the pelvic enhancer PelA, with changes in a second enhancer, PelB, goes with loss of Pitx1 from the developing pelvis. The Pitx1 protein and its jaw expression are kept.
cards.quote: In Paxton fish, a deletion in the pelvic enhancer PelA, with changes in a second enhancer, PelB, goes with the loss of Pitx1 from the developing pelvis

cards.front: Why can losing a pelvic enhancer shrink the stickleback pelvis more safely than losing the Pitx1 protein?
cards.back: Losing the protein removes Pitx1 wherever it works, including the jaw. Losing pelvic enhancer activity shrinks one body part and spares the gene's other jobs.
cards.quote: Losing the protein outright would remove Pitx1 wherever it works; losing pelvic enhancer activity can shrink one body part and spare the gene's other jobs.

cards.front: How far does the Pitx1 enhancer story in threespine sticklebacks generalise?
cards.back: It is the best-studied route to pelvic reduction, found in many but not all reduced populations and explaining much of the trait, not all. It is not a claim that form mostly evolves this way.
cards.quote: It is not a claim that form mostly evolves this way.

cards.front: The stickleback pelvis is {{c1::homologous}} to the tetrapod hip girdle and hind limb: inherited, modified, from a common ancestor.
cards.quote: Its pelvis is homologous to the tetrapod hip girdle and hind limb: inherited, modified, from a common ancestor
cards.section: The puzzle: a lost pelvis with a working gene

cards.front: Mice with no working Pitx1 protein: what happens to them, and what does it say about breaking the protein as a route to pelvic loss?
cards.back: They have malformed hind limbs among other defects and die at or shortly after birth. Pitx1, a transcription factor, works in several places, so a broken protein is a poor route.
cards.quote: mice with no working Pitx1 have malformed hind limbs among other defects and die at or shortly after birth
cards.section: The puzzle: a lost pelvis with a working gene

cards.front: In the 2004 stickleback crosses, pelvic reduction mapped to how many chromosome regions, and where was the major one?
cards.back: One major and four minor regions; the major one lies near Pitx1.
cards.quote: pelvic reduction in their stickleback crosses mapped to one major and four minor chromosome regions, the major one near Pitx1
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: Outline the steps of linkage mapping between two forms of a species.
cards.back: Cross the two forms to make F1 hybrids; intercross the F1 to make an F2 in which parental chromosomes are shuffled; find regions whose genotype travels with the trait.
cards.quote: The method is linkage mapping: cross the two forms to make F1 hybrids, breed them together to make an F2 generation
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: Dominant means {{c1::one copy}} shows the effect; recessive means it takes two.
cards.quote: Dominant means one copy shows the effect; recessive means it takes two.
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: Invented stickleback F2 data, marker beside Pitx1 (M = marine, P = Paxton): 2 of 100 MM, 6 of 200 MP and 32 of 100 PP fish have a reduced pelvis. Compute the frequency in each genotype and state the dominance of the Paxton allele.
cards.back: MM 2/100 = 2%; MP 6/200 = 3%; PP 32/100 = 32%. One Paxton copy barely changes the frequency, two raise it sharply: the region acts close to recessively.
cards.quote: One Paxton copy (MP) barely changes the frequency; two raise it from 2% to 32%.
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: Same invented F2 (2 of 100 MM, 6 of 200 MP, 32 of 100 PP reduced). What share of reduced fish are PP, what share of PP fish are not reduced, and what does the second number imply?
cards.back: Reduced total = 2 + 6 + 32 = 40; 32/40 = 80% are PP. 68 of 100 PP fish (68%) are not reduced, so other loci or the environment matter too.
cards.quote: But 68 of the 100 PP fish are not reduced, so other loci or the environment matter too.
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: In an F2 cross, 8 fish with a reduced pelvis carry at least one marine allele at the marker beside the major locus. Give two explanations.
cards.back: Other factors (other loci or the environment) caused their reduction, or a crossover separated the marker from the causal change.
cards.quote: those other factors, or a crossover between the marker and the causal change, could explain them.
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: A cross maps a trait to a chromosome region that holds many genes, one of them a plausible candidate. Has the cross shown what changed?
cards.back: No. A mapped region tells you where to look, not what changed; it can hold many genes, and further tests must identify the causal sequence.
cards.quote: A mapped region tells you where to look, not what changed: it can hold many genes.
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: What did sequencing of Pitx1 coding sequence show in the pelvic-reduced sticklebacks examined in 2004?
cards.back: No coding mutation changed the encoded Pitx1 protein sequence.
cards.quote: No coding mutation changed the encoded Pitx1 protein sequence in the pelvic-reduced fish they examined.
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: Distinguish a cis change from a trans change in a gene's regulation.
cards.back: Cis: travels with that copy of the DNA and affects only it (a broken switch wired to one lamp). Trans: acts through a diffusible product on every copy in the cell (a power cut dimming every lamp).
cards.quote: a trans change, acting through a diffusible product on every Pitx1 copy in the cell, like a power cut that dims every lamp in the house
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: Why can linkage mapping alone not tell a cis change at Pitx1 from a trans change?
cards.back: The gene for the trans regulator could sit in the same mapped region, so both possibilities give the same mapping result.
cards.quote: Mapping cannot tell these apart, since the regulator's gene could sit in the same region.
cards.section: Mapping: one major region, four minor

cards.front: Measuring how much RNA of one gene comes from each of the two alleles in a hybrid, tissue by tissue, is called {{c1::allele-specific expression}}.
cards.quote: Measure how much Pitx1 RNA comes from each allele (allele-specific expression), tissue by tissue.
cards.section: Cis or trans: the F1 test

cards.front: Why does comparing each allele's RNA in an F1 hybrid separate a cis change from a trans change?
cards.back: Both alleles sit in one nucleus, bathed by the same regulators. A trans change would affect both alike, so a steady unequal share must lie in one allele's own DNA: a cis change.
cards.quote: An F1 hybrid cell holds one marine and one Paxton allele in one nucleus, bathed by the same regulators.
cards.section: Cis or trans: the F1 test

cards.front: Suppose Paxton sticklebacks lack a regulator of Pitx1 in the pelvis (a trans change). In a marine x Paxton F1 pelvic bud, what share of Pitx1 RNA comes from each allele?
cards.back: About 50:50. The F1 cell's regulators act on both alleles alike, so a trans change cannot make one allele lower than the other.
cards.quote: The F1 cell's regulators act on both alleles alike, so a trans change cannot make one allele lower than the other.
cards.section: Cis or trans: the F1 test

cards.front: In marine x Paxton F1 stickleback larvae, 90% of pelvic Pitx1 transcripts come from the marine allele and 10% from the Paxton allele; in the jaw the split is 50:50. Interpret.
cards.back: A cis change on the Paxton allele, specific to the pelvis of the two tissues tested. The alleles share one trans environment, and the jaw shows no defect.
cards.quote: The alleles share one trans environment, so a 90:10 ratio means the Paxton allele itself is less active: a cis change.
cards.section: Cis or trans: the F1 test

cards.front: An F1 test places a pelvic expression difference on one Pitx1 allele (cis). Where in that allele could the difference lie?
cards.back: In an enhancer, in the promoter (where transcription starts) or in the RNA itself. Reporter tests ask which sequence.
cards.quote: It could lie in an enhancer, the promoter (where transcription starts) or the RNA itself
cards.section: Cis or trans: the F1 test

cards.front: In F1 pelvis, a Paxton Pitx1 copy makes 10 RNA molecules for every 90 from a marine copy. Assuming a purely cis change, estimate pelvic Pitx1 RNA in MP and PP fish relative to marine MM fish.
cards.back: Paxton copy = 10/90 ≈ 0.11 of a marine copy. MP = (1 + 0.11)/2 ≈ 56% of marine; PP ≈ 11%.
cards.why: Purely cis means each allele's output does not depend on its partner, so outputs add.
cards.quote: An MP fish, like the F1, makes (1 + 0.11) / 2, about 56% of the marine level; a PP fish about 11%.
cards.section: Cis or trans: the F1 test

cards.front: In the invented stickleback data, MP fish make about 56% of marine pelvic Pitx1 RNA, and pelvic reduction is 2% in MM, 3% in MP and 32% in PP. How can the expression data explain the near-recessive pattern?
cards.back: If one marine copy is nearly enough, over half the marine dose keeps MP pelvises near normal, while PP fish at about 11% fall short. This is an inference from invented numbers, not something they show.
cards.quote: Over half the marine dose would fit the near-recessive pattern if one marine copy is nearly enough
cards.section: Cis or trans: the F1 test

cards.front: Deleting the PelB enhancer in mice left hind-limb Pitx1 RNA at about 85% of control. What does this show about PelB?
cards.back: PelB supplies part of the limb's Pitx1 expression and other enhancers the rest; it is not an on-off switch.
cards.quote: Deleting it in mice trimmed hind-limb Pitx1 expression rather than abolishing it, so PelB supplies part of the limb's Pitx1 expression and other enhancers the rest
cards.section: Enhancers on trial: a second switch, and why the first keeps breaking

cards.front: In mice, patellae were lost only when a PelB deletion sat opposite a Pitx1 null allele, not in PelB-deletion homozygotes. What does this suggest?
cards.back: PelB's partial contribution shows a strong effect only on a sensitized background, where overall Pitx1 dose is already lowered by the null allele.
cards.quote: Patellae were absent only in mice carrying the PelB deletion on one chromosome and a Pitx1 null allele on the other, a sensitized background.
cards.section: PelB in mice and in sticklebacks

cards.front: What is positive selection?
cards.back: A variant spreading because it helps its carriers.
cards.quote: positive selection (a variant spreading because it helps its carriers)
cards.section: Enhancers on trial: a second switch, and why the first keeps breaking

cards.front: What genetic signs of positive selection were found around the Pel enhancer in pelvic-reduced stickleback populations?
cards.back: An excess of derived alleles (newer variants, not ancestral ones) and reduced genetic diversity, not seen in pelvis-complete lake populations.
cards.quote: an excess of derived alleles (newer variants, not the ancestral ones) and reduced genetic diversity not seen in pelvis-complete lake populations
cards.section: Enhancers on trial: a second switch, and why the first keeps breaking

cards.front: The same stickleback enhancer, Pel, is lost in lake after lake. How can mutation and selection both contribute?
cards.back: Mutation may explain why Pel deletions arise again and again; selection why they spread.
cards.why: The Pel sequence breaks easily in a yeast chromosome assay, a clue to recurrence, though that is a yeast result, not a fish mutation rate.
cards.quote: mutation may explain why Pel deletions arise again and again, selection why they spread
cards.section: Enhancers on trial: a second switch, and why the first keeps breaking

cards.front: State the question each method answers: linkage mapping, in situ hybridization, the F1 allele-specific expression test, a reporter assay.
cards.back: Mapping localises; in situ hybridization shows where transcript is; the F1 test detects a cis difference; a reporter shows what a sequence can drive.
cards.quote: mapping localises, in situ hybridization shows where transcript is, the F1 test detects a cis difference, a reporter shows what a sequence can drive
cards.section: What stays open

cards.front: A lab wants to know whether stickleback pelvic form depends on the Pel sequence in the fish's own genome. Which method answers this, and why does a reporter assay fall short?
cards.back: A native-locus edit (deletion or replacement). A reporter shows only what a sequence can drive, not whether form depends on it in place.
cards.quote: a native-locus edit tests whether form depends on the sequence
cards.section: What stays open

cards.front: A Pitx1 minigene driven by marine Pel is injected into eggs of a pelvic-reduced population, and pelvic spines develop variably better than in uninjected siblings. What does this rescue show, and what does it leave untested?
cards.back: Adding Pel-driven Pitx1 can variably enhance pelvic spine development in that population. It does not test whether form depends on the native Pel sequence; that needs a native-locus edit.
cards.quote: rescue asks whether adding it back restores form
cards.section: What stays open

cards.front: Signals of positive selection surround the Pel region in pelvic-reduced sticklebacks. Why do they not identify the trait or ecological pressure selected?
cards.back: A sweep marks a linked region, so it does not show which variant or trait was the direct target, or which pressure acted in a given lake.
cards.quote: Because a sweep marks a linked region, they do not show which variant or trait was the direct target
cards.section: What stays open

cards.front: A survey finds deletions around the Pel enhancer in 9 of 13 pelvic-reduced stickleback populations and in none of 21 pelvis-complete ones. What does this support, and what does it not?
cards.back: Loss of Pel recurs with pelvic reduction. It is not universal: 4 reduced populations lack it, so not every reduced population need carry the same lesion.
cards.quote: Pel deletions are common but not universal among pelvic-reduced populations
cards.section: What stays open

cards.front: What did a 2023 study of sticklebacks in two small Norwegian lakes find at the Pitx1 pelvic enhancers?
cards.back: No obvious association between PelA variants and pelvic status in the lake with spineless fish, and no variation in PelB.
cards.quote: found no obvious association between PelA variants and pelvic status in the lake where spineless fish occur
cards.section: The 2023 Norwegian lakes

cards.front: A pelvic-reduced stickleback population shows no Pel deletion and no association at Pel. Using a cross and the F1 test, how could you ask whether Pitx1 regulation is still involved?
cards.back: Cross to marine fish and check in the F2 whether the region near Pitx1 travels with reduction. Then measure F1 allele-specific Pitx1 expression in pelvic tissue: an unequal share points to another cis lesion at Pitx1; 50:50 in the pelvic tissue tested argues against one there.
cards.why: Rests on the F1 rule: only a difference in one allele's own DNA can make its share unequal.
cards.quote: Only a difference in one allele's own DNA can, so an unequal share in one tissue only points to a tissue-specific cis change.
cards.section: Cis or trans: the F1 test

cards.front: Paxton sticklebacks carry changes in both PelA and PelB. Design an experiment to measure each enhancer's contribution to pelvic size.
cards.back: In marine fish, edit the native locus to install the Paxton-type change at PelA alone, PelB alone and both; several independent lines each, unedited sibling controls, raised together, measured blind; measure pelvic Pitx1 RNA too.
cards.why: Reporters cannot split the two enhancers' contributions; only native-locus edits can.
cards.quote: In marine (pelvis-complete) fish, use genome editing to install the Paxton-type change at PelA alone, PelB alone, and both.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a genome-editing experiment, why make several independent edited lines of each genotype?
cards.back: So that one off-target edit cannot explain the result.
cards.quote: Make several independent lines of each (so one off-target edit cannot explain the result)
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Invented data: control stickleback pelvic spine length 10 units; PelA edit alone 8; PelB edit alone 9; double edit 4. Are the effects additive?
cards.back: Additive expectation: double = PelA + PelB − control = 8 + 9 − 10 = 7. Observed 4 is a larger loss (6 vs 3), so the edits interact.
cards.why: If effects add on the length scale, the double edit's loss is about the sum of the single losses.
cards.quote: the double edit's loss is about the sum of the single losses (double = PelA alone + PelB alone − control)
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a PelA/PelB editing experiment, the double edit removes the pelvis entirely and its loss is smaller than the sum of the single losses. Why is this weak evidence of interaction?
cards.back: A fish with no pelvis left cannot lose more. That floor caps the measured loss and can mimic an interaction.
cards.quote: A fish with no pelvis left cannot lose more, and that floor can mimic an interaction.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Invented stickleback data, ratios Paxton over marine pelvic Pitx1 RNA: F1 allele ratio 0.11; parents' ratio 0.05. Assuming cis and trans effects multiply, estimate the trans effect.
cards.back: Parents' ratio = cis × trans, with cis = F1 ratio. Trans = 0.05 / 0.11 ≈ 0.45. (A parents' ratio of 0.11 would give trans = 1.0, none.)
cards.quote: If cis and trans effects multiply, parents' ratio = cis × trans
cards.section: What the F1 test does and does not separate

cards.front: In a hybrid, two alleles of a gene give a 50:50 RNA split, yet the parent carrying one of them makes much less of that RNA than the other parent. What kind of change explains the parental difference?
cards.back: A trans change (assuming cis and trans effects multiply and like tissues are compared). Equal F1 shares mean no cis difference, so the parents differ in regulators acting on every copy.
cards.quote: To ask whether trans factors add to it, compare the parents
cards.section: What the F1 test does and does not separate

cards.front: Why was the PelB enhancer, rather than PelA, tested by deletion in mice?
cards.back: PelA is not conserved in mammals.
cards.quote: Because PelA is not conserved in mammals, Thompson and colleagues tested PelB in mice
cards.section: PelB in mice and in sticklebacks

cards.front: How did the Paxton benthic PelB reporter compare with the marine PelB reporter in sticklebacks?
cards.back: It drove weaker, more restricted pelvic expression while keeping strong jaw expression.
cards.quote: its reporter drove weaker, more restricted pelvic expression than the marine one while keeping strong jaw expression
cards.section: PelB in mice and in sticklebacks
